content: 1. For infants less than 4 weeks of age, pharmacokinetic data is only available for zidovudine (AZT). There is significant uncertainty regarding the appropriate dosing of nevirapine (NVP), raltegravir (RAL), and lamivudine (3TC) in preterm and low birth weight infants. 2. Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) solution should not be administered to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age due to the risk of adverse effects in this population. 3. LPV/r solution should not be used in infants younger than 2 weeks of age. Additionally, LPV/r pellets should not be used in infants younger than 3 months of age. 4. For children receiving rifampicin-containing tuberculosis treatment, ritonavir (RTV) super-boosting is recommended to achieve a 1:1 dose ratio with LPV. This dosing approach is supported by studies in young children receiving LPV/r. 5. The heat-stable tablet formulation of LPV/r must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. 6. Ritonavir liquid requires a cold chain for transport and storage. 7. LPV/r pellet formulations should not be used in infants younger than 3 months of age. 8. The dosing schedule provided applies to equivalent solid dosage forms, such as LPV/r granules, that may become available. 9. Ritonavir oral solution dosing is based on the dosing tested in trials supporting the use of super-boosting. 10. In recent years, improved antiretroviral (ARV) formulations, such as dispersible and scored fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets, have replaced traditional liquid formulations. These products have simplified pediatric HIV care delivery in low-income settings. 11. However, the proliferation of options has led to a multiplicity of formulations across regimens and weight bands, creating challenges in procurement and supply chain management. 12. Generic manufacturers rely on economies of scale to maintain affordable pricing, but demand fragmentation across too many duplicative products destabilizes the reliable supply of pediatric ARV dosage forms. 13. The ARV Procurement Working Group (APWG) and the Global Accelerator for Pediatric Formulations (GAP-f) provide formulary guidance to programs on selecting optimal pediatric ARVs based on robust criteria. 14. The Optimal Pediatric ARV Formulary currently includes eight products that deliver recommended firstand second-line regimens across all pediatric weight bands. 15. The formulary, first developed in 2011, is routinely revised to align with current WHO guidelines and available products. Programs are encouraged to procure pediatric dosage forms included in the Optimal Pediatric ARV Formulary. 16. During transitions or special circumstances (e.g., neonatal treatment, tuberculosis co-treatment, and third-line regimens), dosage forms included in the ARV Limited-Use Formulary provide appropriate coverage. 17. There is an urgent need for better age-appropriate formulations for infants and children living with HIV. Several solid formulations are in the final stages of development, including ABC/3TC/LPV/r granules, ABC/3TC/EFV, and DTG 10 mg scored dispersible tablets. 18. The availability of co-formulated DRV/r in heat-stable fixed-dose combination formulations is critical to facilitate treatment sequencing and uptake of future secondand third-line treatments. 19. Additional formulations containing newer drugs, such as dolutegravir (DTG) and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), are being prioritized to optimize dosing, sequencing, and harmonization across age groups. 20. Simplified dosing for formulations under development has been outlined by the Pediatric Antiretroviral Drug Optimization (PADO) group based on the best available information. However, optimal dosing of DTG in children below 25 kg is still under investigation, and proposed dosing will be revised as more evidence becomes available. 21. Scored tablets with doubled-strength components (e.g., ABC/3TC/DTG 120/60/10 mg) could reduce pill burden for children, but challenges in ensuring accurate dosing when scoring a triple-drug FDC must be addressed. 22. For early infant diagnosis (EID) of HIV, the key principles include assessing HIV exposure status through maternal antibody testing, performing nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HIV-exposed children with clinical symptoms, and ensuring confirmatory testing following any positive result. 23. Indeterminate test results should be repeat-tested immediately and given priority for rapid resolution. A team of experts should review repeated indeterminate results to determine the best follow-up care. 24. For HIV-exposed newborns, NAT can be considered at birth. If positive, ART should be initiated immediately, and NAT should be repeated to confirm infection. 25. For HIV-exposed infants aged 4–6 weeks to 18 months, NAT should be conducted at the earliest opportunity. If positive, ART should be started immediately, and NAT should be repeated to confirm infection. 26. Regular clinical monitoring and follow-up are essential for all HIV-exposed infants until a final diagnosis is made, including providing co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and clinical and nutritional assessments. 27. For infants who are breastfed, the risk of acquiring HIV remains until breastfeeding cessation. Retesting at 18 months or three months after breastfeeding cessation (whichever is later) is necessary for final assessment of HIV status. 28. For infants younger than 18 months, NAT should be performed to confirm infection. For children older than 18 months, negative antibody testing confirms the child is uninfected, while positive antibody testing confirms infection.
